The first scrap lies beneath a paper layer, while the second is suspended above the glass. When a green field is introduced underneath the glass, both scraps exhibit contrast due to differential illumination. This phenomenon is governed by the interplay of simultaneous induction and edge interference. Simultaneous induction causes fading of contrast over time under sustained fixation, modeled as an exponential decay process. Edge interference introduces variability in contrast visibility based on the physical properties of the scraps' boundaries—specifically their brightness and texture. Accommodation dependence further modulates this perception by altering how the eye focuses on the stimuli, introducing directional bias in contrast interpretation. These three operators form a hierarchical system where edge interference sets initial conditions, accommodation determines the observer's perspective, and simultaneous induction governs temporal evolution. The failure mode occurs when environmental factors such as lighting inconsistency or improper positioning disrupt the controlled experimental setup, leading to unreliable data.
